---
title: "Beam Search"
description: "A decoding algorithm that keeps several high-scoring partial sequences while generating output."
term: "Beam Search"
letter: "B"
category: "NLP"
difficulty: "Intermediate"

## Simple explanation

Beam search generates a sequence by keeping several promising partial
answers at once. At each step, it expands those candidates and keeps the
best-scoring ones instead of committing to only one next token.

## Technical explanation

For a beam width $k$, the decoder retains up to $k$ partial sequences,
scores expansions using model probabilities or a related objective, and
prunes candidates to keep the beam bounded. Length normalization and
constraints may be used because raw sequence log-probabilities tend to
favour shorter outputs.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Beam search is used in sequence-generation tasks such as translation and
speech recognition. It trades additional computation for broader search,
but a larger beam does not necessarily yield more useful or human-preferred
output.

## How it works

The decoder initializes a beam with a start token, expands each candidate
with possible next tokens, scores the resulting sequences, and keeps the
top $k$. It repeats until candidates finish or a stopping condition is
met.

## Practical example

A translation model can keep several possible partial translations after
each generated token. If one early choice leads to a poor continuation,
another candidate may still produce a better complete translation.

## Common misconceptions

- Beam search is not the same as exhaustive search over every possible
  sequence.
- A higher-scoring sequence under the model is not necessarily the most
  accurate or natural output.
- Beam width alone does not determine output quality; scoring and stopping
  rules also matter.
